deep.reconstruction:
Context (p.222). The ellipse has semi-axes 1+λ and 1−λ. A boundary point is z = (1+λ)cos e + i(1−λ)sin e = u + λ/u, with u = e^{ie}, so e is the eccentric anomaly. For two boundary points (e,u) and (E,U), log|z_U − z_u| = Re[log(U−u) + log(1 − λ/(uU))]. Gauss expands this in cosines of (E−e) and of (E+e). If mass is spread on the ellipse with density A + Σ(A_n cos ne + B_n sin ne) per de, its logarithmic potential at boundary point E is −π Σ (1/n)[(1+λ^n)A_n cos nE + (1−λ^n)B_n sin nE]. If instead the mass 2πA sits at the centre, its potential is Re 2πA log(U + λ/U) = 2πA Σ_k (−1)^{k+1}(λ^k/k) cos 2kE.

This page.

(1) Equating the two boundary potentials. Only even cosine terms can match, with n = 2k:
−π(1/2k)(1+λ^{2k})A_{2k} = 2πA(−1)^{k+1}λ^k/k.
Hence A_{2k} = 4A(−1)^k λ^k/(1+λ^{2k}), and the required density is
A de [1 − 4λ/(1+λ²) cos2e + 4λ²/(1+λ⁴) cos4e − 4λ³/(1+λ⁶) cos6e …].
In modern terms this is the balayage of the central point mass onto the ellipse, i.e. the harmonic measure of the ellipse interior seen from its centre.

(2) Writing the mass as A dp with p(0)=0 and integrating termwise:
p = e − 2λ/(1+λ²) sin2e + (2/2)·λ²/(1+λ⁴) sin4e − (2/3)·λ³/(1+λ⁶) sin6e …
Gauss says this agrees with the formula of 'S.177' (an earlier section, not visible) if ip is the imaginary part of log t.

(3) Definition of t. log t is the complete complex potential (real plus imaginary part) of the central mass minus that of the distributed mass, normalised by 2πA, at the point z = u + λ/u. Gauss states
log t = log u − Σ_k (−1)^{k+1} λ^k/(k(1+λ^{2k})) (u^{2k} − u^{−2k}).
On |u| = 1 we have u^{2k} − u^{−2k} = 2i sin 2ke, so log t = ip there. The real part vanishes (the potentials agree) and |t| = 1; hence 'die obige Reihe selbst'.

(4) Product form. Gauss writes
t = u · (1+λu^{−2})/(1+λu²) · (1+λ³u²)/(1+λ³u^{−2}) · (1+λ⁵u^{−2})/(1+λ⁵u²) ⋯
That is, factors ((1+λ^j u^{−2})/(1+λ^j u²))^{ε_j} over odd j, with ε_j = +1 for j ≡ 1 and −1 for j ≡ 3 (mod 4).
Verification (mine): take logs and expand. The coefficient of (−1)^{k+1}(u^{−2k} − u^{2k})/k is Σ_j ε_j λ^{jk} = x − x³ + x⁵ − … with x = λ^k, which equals λ^k/(1+λ^{2k}). This reproduces (3).

(5) Theta-quotient form, with μ² = λ.
t = Σ_n μ^{(2n)²}(μu)^{2n} / Σ_{n odd} μ^{n²}(μu)^n,
i.e. an even-index theta series over an odd-index one (q = μ, argument μu). Multiplying out:
t = u · (1 + μ²u^{−2} + μ⁶u² + μ¹²u^{−4} + μ²⁰u⁴ + …) / (1 + μ²u² + μ⁶u^{−2} + μ¹²u⁴ + μ²⁰u^{−4} + …).
The general terms are λ^{2n²+n}u^{2n} in the numerator and λ^{2n²−n}u^{2n} in the denominator.
Verification (mine), by the Jacobi triple product with Q = λ²:
• numerator = Π(1−λ^{4m})(1+λ^{4m−1}u²)(1+λ^{4m−3}u^{−2}),
• denominator = Π(1−λ^{4m})(1+λ^{4m−3}u²)(1+λ^{4m−1}u^{−2}).
The quotient is exactly the product in (4).

Meaning (my interpretation, supported by p.224). From the series, t(1/u) = 1/t(u); p.224 adds t(λu)t(u) = 1. Together these give t(λ/u) = t(u), so t is a single-valued function of z inside the ellipse. It is analytic there and vanishes at z = 0 (u = i√λ kills the factor 1+λu^{−2}). It has |t| = 1 on the ellipse, and log|t| is the Green function of the ellipse with pole at the centre. Hence t(z) is the conformal map of the ellipse interior onto the unit disk with centre → 0, expressed by theta functions. Page 224 confirms this with du/u = dT/√(T²−4λ), where T = z, plus elliptic differential relations.
errors: No mathematical errors found: the coefficients, the integration to p, the product, and both theta forms all check out.

Minor imprecision: log t is defined by a series that converges for √λ < |u| < 1/√λ. Calling it the 'complete potential' difference at a point *on* the ellipse implicitly takes boundary values of an analytic function; this is not justified on the page.
The constant (A-)term of the distributed potential is silently taken as 0 (true, since the mean of log|U−u| over |u|=1 vanishes for |U|=1). This is only implicit.

results.what: Density on an ellipse whose log-potential on the boundary equals that of the same mass at the centre: A(1 + Σ 4(−1)^kλ^k/(1+λ^{2k}) cos 2ke) in the eccentric anomaly.
results.modern_name: Harmonic measure of the ellipse interior from its centre (balayage / Poisson kernel of the ellipse)
results.usually_credited_to: Implicit in 19th-c. potential theory (Green 1828, Dirichlet problem for ellipse via elliptic coordinates); explicit series form unsure

results.what: t(u) = u Π_{j odd}((1+λ^j u^{-2})/(1+λ^j u^2))^{±1} = quotient of theta series; |t|=1 on the ellipse, t(0)=0. This is the conformal map of the ellipse onto the unit disk.
results.modern_name: Conformal (Riemann) map of an ellipse interior onto the disk via elliptic/theta functions

results.what: Equality of the infinite product with the theta-series quotient.
results.usually_credited_to: Jacobi 1829 (Gauss known to have had it earlier in his Nachlass)

results.what: Log-distance expansion for confocal ellipses via z = u + λ/u.
results.modern_name: Joukowski map / Fourier expansion of logarithmic kernel in elliptic coordinates

deep.surprise_reason: Taken together with p.224, Gauss constructs the Green function and conformal disk map of an ellipse explicitly as a theta quotient. This result is usually attributed to Schwarz (1869). Gauss's theta and triple-product work is well known, and he does not explicitly state conformality on this page, so it is notable but not revolutionary. I am unsure whether Schlesinger or the editors of the Werke already discussed this note.
